items.stem: A Lorenz curve shows
options: the relationship between unemployment and inflation
the cumulative percentage of income received by cumulative percentages of the population
income per head over time
the share of each sector in GDP
items.answer: the cumulative percentage of income received by cumulative percentages of the population
items.markingKey: Plotted against the 45° line of perfect equality.

items.stem: Distinguish between income and wealth.
items.answer: Income is a flow of money received over a period (wages, rent, interest, profit, benefits); wealth is a stock of assets owned at a point in time (property, shares, savings).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain one limitation of the Gini coefficient as a measure of inequality.
items.answer: Different Lorenz curves can give the same Gini, so it does not show where in the distribution inequality occurs; it ignores non-cash benefits and household size.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: limitation; 1 mark: explanation [2]

items.stem: Income shares by quintile (poorest first) in Korvia are: quintile 1: 6%, quintile 2: 14%, quintile 3: 22%, quintile 4: 27%, quintile 5: 31%. Calculate the cumulative share of income received by the poorest 80% of households.
items.markingKey: Sum of first 4 quintiles: 6 + 14 + 22 + 27 = 69%.

items.stem: Income shares by quintile (poorest first) in Marvona: quintile 1: 4%, quintile 2: 14%, quintile 3: 21%, quintile 4: 24%, quintile 5: 37%. (a) Calculate the cumulative income shares for plotting a Lorenz curve. (b) Using the trapezium rule, estimate the Gini coefficient.
items.markingKey: (a) cumulative shares [2]; (b) B = Σ 0.2 × (Yᵢ + Yᵢ₋₁)/2 = 0.348 [2]; G = A/(A + B) with A + B = 0.5 → 0.3 [1].

items.stem: Income shares by quintile (poorest first) in Istrana: quintile 1: 8%, quintile 2: 16%, quintile 3: 20%, quintile 4: 26%, quintile 5: 30%. (a) Calculate the cumulative income shares for plotting a Lorenz curve. (b) Using the trapezium rule, estimate the Gini coefficient. (c) After a reform, the poorest 20% gained a 3 percentage point higher share at the expense of the richest 20%. Explain how the Lorenz curve and Gini coefficient would change.
items.answer: (a) 20%: 8%, 40%: 24%, 60%: 44%, 80%: 70%, 100%: 100% (b) Area under Lorenz curve B = 0.392; Gini = (0.5 − 0.392)/0.5 = 0.22. (c) The Lorenz curve moves closer to the line of equality and the Gini coefficient falls.
items.markingKey: (a) cumulative shares [2]; (b) B = Σ 0.2 × (Yᵢ + Yᵢ₋₁)/2 = 0.392 [2]; G = A/(A + B) with A + B = 0.5 → 0.22 [1]. (c) direction of movement and Gini fall [2].

items.stem: Extract: In Tarvia, the poorest 20% of households receive 4% of income and the richest 20% receive 39%. Quintile shares are 4%, 14%, 19%, 24%, 39%. The government proposes higher top tax rates and a rise in means-tested benefits. (a) Calculate the ratio of the income share of the richest quintile to the poorest quintile. (b) Estimate the Gini coefficient using the trapezium method.

Extract: In Quentara, the poorest 20% of households receive 6% of income and the richest 20% receive 38%. Quintile shares are 6%, 13%, 17%, 26%, 38%. The government proposes higher top tax rates and a rise in means-tested benefits. (a) Calculate the ratio of the income share of the richest quintile to the poorest quintile. (b) Explain how the proposals would change the Lorenz curve. (c) Explain one reason why higher top tax rates may raise less revenue than expected.
items.answer: (a) 6.33 (b) Higher top taxes and more benefits raise the poor’s share and reduce the rich’s, moving the curve towards the line of equality. (c) Tax avoidance and evasion, migration of high earners, reduced work effort (Laffer curve).

items.stem: A Gini coefficient of 0 indicates
options: zero income
perfect equality of income
a balanced budget
perfect inequality
items.answer: perfect equality of income
items.markingKey: Gini ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has all income).

items.stem: Explain how progressive taxation affects the Lorenz curve.
items.answer: Taking a larger proportion of higher incomes reduces post-tax income shares of the rich relative to the poor, moving the Lorenz curve towards the line of equality and lowering the Gini.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: higher proportion from rich; 1 mark: curve moves towards equality [2]

items.stem: The Gini coefficient in Selmaria has risen from 0.32 to 0.41 over twenty years. (a) Explain how a Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient are used to measure inequality. (b) Discuss whether the Gini coefficient is the best measure of inequality in an economy.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Single summary figure, comparable across countries and time. (b) Case for the view: Single summary figure, comparable across countries and time. Case against / evaluation: Same Gini from different curves; ignores wealth, non-cash benefits, household size and regional prices; quintile ratios and Palma ratio add information. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: Absolute poverty is
options: having less income than the average person
being unemployed
a situation where income is too low to meet basic needs such as food, shelter and clothing
paying more tax than others
items.answer: a situation where income is too low to meet basic needs such as food, shelter and clothing
items.markingKey: Often measured by an international line such as $2.15 a day (PPP).

items.stem: Distinguish between absolute and relative poverty.
items.answer: Absolute: income insufficient for basic needs, a fixed standard; relative: income low compared with others in the same society (e.g. below 60% of median), so it changes as average incomes rise.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain how means-tested benefits can create a poverty trap.
items.answer: As income rises, means-tested benefits are withdrawn, which together with income tax creates a high effective marginal tax rate, so the gain from working more is small and work incentives fall.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: benefit withdrawal; 1 mark: high EMTR; 1 mark: work disincentive [3]

items.stem: Daniel works part-time and receives a means-tested benefit. A pay rise adds $100 a week to gross income. Income tax is 20%, social insurance contributions are 8% and the benefit is withdrawn at 60% of extra gross income. Calculate Daniel’s effective marginal tax rate.

Sofia works part-time and receives a means-tested benefit. A pay rise adds $50 a week to gross income. Income tax is 10%, social insurance contributions are 10% and the benefit is withdrawn at 55% of extra gross income. Calculate the increase in Sofia’s net income and the effective marginal tax rate, and explain whether this is a poverty trap.
items.answer: Change in net income = $12.50 a week; EMTR = 75%. Yes: over half of the extra income is lost, weakening the incentive to work more.
items.markingKey: Lost = 50 × 75% = 37.5 [1]; net gain = 12.5 [1]; EMTR 75% [1]; poverty trap explained [1].

items.stem: Extract: In Ostrelia, the poorest 20% of households receive 14% of income and the richest 20% receive 25%. Quintile shares are 14%, 18%, 21%, 22%, 25%. The government proposes higher top tax rates and a rise in means-tested benefits. (a) Calculate the ratio of the income share of the richest quintile to the poorest quintile. (b) Estimate the Gini coefficient using the trapezium method.
Relative poverty is commonly defined as
options: income below $2.15 a day
income below the minimum wage
household income below 60% of median income
having no wealth
items.answer: household income below 60% of median income
items.markingKey: Relative measure: poverty compared with the living standards of the society.

items.stem: Explain why relative poverty may rise even when absolute poverty falls.
items.answer: If the incomes of the poor rise but median income rises faster, more people fall below 60% of median even though fewer lack basic needs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: median rises faster; 1 mark: explanation [2]

items.stem: The weekly incomes of nine households in a survey are ($): 360, 440, 640, 660, 700, 1040, 1060, 1070, 1190. Using a relative poverty line of 60% of median income, calculate the poverty line and the number of households in relative poverty.
items.answer: Median = $700; poverty line = $420; 1 household in relative poverty.
items.markingKey: Median = 5th value = 700 [1]; 0.6 × 700 = 420 [1]; count below: 360 [1].

items.stem: Ravi works part-time and receives a means-tested benefit. A pay rise adds $120 a week to gross income. Income tax is 15%, social insurance contributions are 5% and the benefit is withdrawn at 55% of extra gross income. Calculate the increase in Ravi’s net income and the effective marginal tax rate, and explain whether this is a poverty trap.
items.answer: Change in net income = $30 a week; EMTR = 75%. Yes: over half of the extra income is lost, weakening the incentive to work more.
items.markingKey: Lost = 120 × 75% = 90 [1]; net gain = 30 [1]; EMTR 75% [1]; poverty trap explained [1].

items.stem: A tax is progressive if
options: everyone pays the same amount
it is paid only by firms
the proportion of income paid in tax rises as income rises
the proportion of income paid falls as income rises
items.answer: the proportion of income paid in tax rises as income rises
items.markingKey: Average tax rate rises with income.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the marginal and average rate of tax.
items.answer: Marginal: the tax rate on an extra dollar of income; average: total tax paid divided by total income. In a progressive system the marginal rate exceeds the average rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each; 1 mark relationship [3]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of means-tested benefits compared with universal benefits.
items.answer: Advantage: targeted at those in need, lower cost. Disadvantage: low take-up due to stigma or complexity, administrative cost, poverty trap.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Income tax bands in Sundara are: income up to $12,000: 0%; $12,000–$30,000: 10%; $30,000–$80,000: 20%; above $80,000: 35%. A worker earns $200,000 a year. Calculate the total income tax paid.
items.markingKey: Tax by band = $53,800.

items.stem: Income tax bands in Gorvania are: income up to $12,000: 0%; $12,000–$30,000: 10%; $30,000–$100,000: 25%; above $100,000: 40%. A worker earns $200,000 a year. Calculate the tax paid, the average and the marginal tax rate. Compare with a worker earning $20,000 and explain whether the system is progressive.
items.answer: $200,000: tax $59,300, average rate 29.6%, marginal rate 40%. $20,000: tax $800, average rate 4%. The average rate rises with income, so the system is progressive.
items.markingKey: Tax band by band [2]; average = tax/income [1]; marginal = rate on the next dollar [1]; comparison of average rates → progressive [1].

items.stem: A sales tax of 15% is applied to all goods in Fendaria. Households in the poorest quintile spend 95% of their income; those in the richest spend 50%. Analyse whether the tax is progressive or regressive.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Distinguish between absolute and relative poverty. (b) Explain why relative poverty may rise even when absolute poverty falls.
items.answer: (a) Absolute: income insufficient for basic needs, a fixed standard; relative: income low compared with others in the same society (e.g. below 60% of median), so it changes as average incomes rise. (b) If the incomes of the poor rise but median income rises faster, more people fall below 60% of median even though fewer lack basic needs.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: median rises faster; 1 mark: explanation [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Distinguish between absolute and relative poverty. (b) Explain how means-tested benefits can create a poverty trap.
items.answer: (a) Absolute: income insufficient for basic needs, a fixed standard; relative: income low compared with others in the same society (e.g. below 60% of median), so it changes as average incomes rise. (b) As income rises, means-tested benefits are withdrawn, which together with income tax creates a high effective marginal tax rate, so the gain from working more is small and work incentives fall.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark: benefit withdrawal; 1 mark: high EMTR; 1 mark: work disincentive [3]

items.stem: The weekly incomes of nine households in a survey are ($): 160, 400, 420, 440, 540, 770, 990, 1030, 1090. Using a relative poverty line of 60% of median income, calculate the poverty line and the number of households in relative poverty.
items.answer: Median = $540; poverty line = $324; 1 household in relative poverty.
items.markingKey: Median = 5th value = 540 [1]; 0.6 × 540 = 324 [1]; count below: 160 [1].

items.stem: Ines works part-time and receives a means-tested benefit. A pay rise adds $50 a week to gross income. Income tax is 25%, social insurance contributions are 10% and the benefit is withdrawn at 70% of extra gross income. Calculate the increase in Ines’s net income and the effective marginal tax rate, and explain whether this is a poverty trap.
items.answer: Change in net income = −$2.50 a week; EMTR = 105%. Yes: net income actually falls, so there is no financial incentive to earn more.
items.markingKey: Lost = 50 × 105% = 52.5 [1]; net gain = -2.5 [1]; EMTR 105% [1]; poverty trap explained [1].

items.stem: A report in Esteria found that one household in five is below the relative poverty line. (a) Explain how the poverty trap arises. (b) Discuss the extent to which the poverty trap is the main reason why poverty persists.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: High EMTRs discourage work, keeping people on low incomes. (b) Case for the view: High EMTRs discourage work, keeping people on low incomes. Case against / evaluation: Other causes: low skills, discrimination, ill health, lack of jobs, housing costs; reforms to withdrawal rates help but cost money. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: A universal benefit is one that
options: requires a means test
is paid only to those below an income threshold
is paid only to the unemployed
is paid to everyone in a category regardless of income
items.answer: is paid to everyone in a category regardless of income
items.markingKey: E.g. child benefit for all; simple, high take-up, but costly.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the difference between the marginal and average rate of tax. (b) Explain why a minimum wage may not be an effective way of reducing poverty.
items.answer: (a) Marginal: the tax rate on an extra dollar of income; average: total tax paid divided by total income. In a progressive system the marginal rate exceeds the average rate. (b) Many poor households have no one in work (pensioners, unemployed); some minimum-wage earners live in higher-income households; it may reduce employment if set too high.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each; 1 mark relationship [3] (b) 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of means-tested benefits compared with universal benefits. (b) Explain why a minimum wage may not be an effective way of reducing poverty.
items.answer: (a) Advantage: targeted at those in need, lower cost. Disadvantage: low take-up due to stigma or complexity, administrative cost, poverty trap. (b) Many poor households have no one in work (pensioners, unemployed); some minimum-wage earners live in higher-income households; it may reduce employment if set too high.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: Income tax bands in Zentara are: income up to $12,500: 0%; $12,500–$40,000: 20%; $40,000–$90,000: 40%; above $90,000: 45%. A worker earns $200,000 a year. Calculate the total income tax paid.
items.markingKey: Tax by band = $75,000.

items.stem: Income tax bands in Zentara are: income up to $12,000: 0%; $12,000–$50,000: 15%; $50,000–$100,000: 30%; above $100,000: 45%. A worker earns $60,000 a year. Calculate the tax paid, the average and the marginal tax rate. Compare with a worker earning $250,000 and explain whether the system is progressive.
items.answer: $60,000: tax $8,700, average rate 14.5%, marginal rate 30%. $250,000: tax $88,200, average rate 35.3%. The average rate rises with income, so the system is progressive.
items.markingKey: Tax band by band [2]; average = tax/income [1]; marginal = rate on the next dollar [1]; comparison of average rates → progressive [1].

items.stem: Consider whether the government should aim for complete equality of income.
items.answer: Arguments for: Equity, social cohesion, lower relative poverty. Arguments against / evaluation: Loss of incentives, efficiency costs; equity vs equality; reward for skill and risk. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.
